title: Jobs of Today and Tomorrow: What Will You Do?
paragraphs: When WKU students are asked what they want to do after graduation, the answers are often confident: "I want to work in IT," "I'm going to be a doctor," "I plan to go into finance." What is less common is the follow-up thought: what will those jobs actually look like in ten or fifteen years? The world of work is changing faster than at any other point in history, and the profession you train for today may bear only a partial resemblance to the job you actually do in 2035.

The most significant driver of change is automation. Artificial intelligence and machine learning are not simply replacing routine manual tasks — they are beginning to handle work that was previously considered the exclusive territory of highly educated professionals. Legal research, financial analysis, medical diagnosis, and even creative writing are now being assisted or partially performed by AI systems. The question for university graduates is not whether automation will affect their field, but how, and by how much.

Some jobs are well-positioned to survive and thrive. Work that requires genuine human connection — counselling, teaching, nursing, social work — is difficult to automate because it depends on empathy, trust, and the ability to read complex emotional situations. Work that requires creative problem-solving in novel, unpredictable contexts is similarly resistant. A therapist who listens carefully and a poet who creates something new are both doing something that machines, for the foreseeable future, cannot replicate.

Other fields are transforming in interesting ways. Medicine is not disappearing, but the role of the doctor is changing: AI systems can now read medical scans with accuracy that rivals or exceeds human specialists. This does not mean radiologists will be replaced — it means the best radiologists will be those who can work alongside AI, interpret its outputs critically, and focus their own attention on the cases that require human judgment.

For WKU students studying for careers in IT, engineering, economics, ecology, and education, the message is nuanced. Your technical skills matter — but so does your ability to communicate, collaborate, and think creatively. The graduates who thrive will be those who can do something that AI cannot: synthesise information from different domains, communicate it clearly, and make decisions under genuine uncertainty.

The most honest advice for anyone entering the workforce in the next five years is this: build T-shaped skills. Go deep in one area — develop genuine expertise. But also build breadth — learn to communicate, to understand other fields, to see how your work connects to the wider world. Read widely. Build relationships. Practise disagreeing respectfully and thinking for yourself.

The jobs of the future have not been invented yet. Some of the most valuable work done in 2035 will be done by people in roles that do not currently exist. The best preparation is not to predict which profession will survive — it is to become a person who can adapt.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I've been thinking a lot about what job I'll actually have in ten years.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: It's hard to predict. Do you think AI will change software engineering a lot?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Definitely. But I think the engineers who can work with AI will have MORE work, not less.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Like the radiologist example in the text — humans working alongside machines.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Exactly. The key is to stay adaptable. Keep learning new things even after you graduate.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: The T-shaped skills idea makes sense to me. Deep expertise plus broad communication.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: The question is: what's YOUR depth? What are you going to go deep in?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Linguistics and education technology. That combination doesn't exist yet — which is exactly why it might.

keyPhrases.context: "The most significant driver of change is automation." = using machines to replace human work.
"For the foreseeable future, machines cannot replicate this." = in the near future we can see.
"Build T-shaped skills." = deep in one area + broad knowledge of others.
"Synthesise information from different domains." = combine ideas from different areas.
"The message is nuanced." = complex, with many different aspects.
"Develop genuine expertise." = deep, real knowledge and skill in a field.
"AI can read scans with accuracy that rivals specialists." = equals or exceeds.
"Become a person who can adapt." = change and adjust to new situations.

vocab.definition: the use of machines or computers to do work previously done by people
vocab.example: Automation is changing which jobs exist — and what those jobs involve.

vocab.definition: a high level of knowledge or skill in a particular field
vocab.example: "Develop genuine expertise." — deep, real mastery of a subject.

vocab.definition: to combine information from different sources into a whole
vocab.example: The best graduates can synthesise ideas from different fields.

vocab.definition: showing small and subtle differences; not simple
vocab.example: "The message is nuanced." — there are many complex factors to consider.

vocab.definition: to copy or reproduce something exactly
vocab.example: Machines cannot replicate the empathy of a good counsellor.

vocab.definition: certain to happen; impossible to avoid
vocab.example: It is inevitable that automation will affect some careers.

vocab.definition: able to change and adjust to new conditions
vocab.example: The best preparation is to become an adaptable person.

vocab.definition: the wide range of something; extent across many areas
vocab.example: "Build breadth" — knowledge across many different fields.
